sections.h2: What homestead exemption means in Connecticut
sections.html:
In Connecticut law, a homestead exemption shields a home from creditors. It is not a discount on the property tax bill. The rule is in section 52-352b of the General Statutes, and it limits what a judgment creditor can reach in a home.

Plenty of people search the phrase hoping to cut a tax bill, but the term means something else here. Tax relief for older, disabled, blind or veteran owners comes from other statutes with other names, covered further down.

sections.h2: How much of a home is protected from creditors
sections.html:
The statute protects the homestead of the exemptioner up to a value of $250,000. Value is the fair market value of the real property less any statutory or consensual lien on it. A smaller limit of $75,000 applies to money judgments that arise from a claim of sexual abuse or exploitation of a minor, sexual assault or other wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct by a natural person.

The number used to be far smaller. A 1993 law (Public Act 93-301) started it at $75,000, a 2003 act added $125,000 for hospital services judgments, and Public Act 21-161 swapped both for $250,000. The larger exemption applies in bankruptcy and postjudgment proceedings begun on or after October 1, 2021, whenever the underlying debt arose.

  • Statute: Conn. Gen. Stat. 52-352b(21).
  • Protected value: $250,000, measured as fair market value minus liens.
  • Reduced amount: $75,000 for the misconduct judgments described above.

Dollar limits get amended, so have a Connecticut attorney confirm today's number.

A homestead is owner-occupied real property, a co-op, or a mobile manufactured home used as a primary residence. That definition is in section 52-352a(5). Public Act 10-181 added co-ops and Public Act 94-55 added mobile manufactured homes.

  • Owner-occupied: a house you rent to someone else is not a homestead for this purpose.
  • Primary residence: a second home or a vacation property does not qualify.
  • Exemptioner: the person claiming the exemption must be a natural person, so a house held in an LLC is outside the definition.

An inherited house you do not live in is not your primary residence, so the shield may not reach it. An attorney can sort out facts like that.

The exemption does not stop a mortgage lender. A mortgage is a consensual lien, and the statute measures the exemption after subtracting liens. Courts have said a mortgage is outside the homestead exemption. One decision also upheld a waiver that the homeowner gave voluntarily with a lawyer's help.

One appellate ruling held that homestead rights attach to the proceeds once a foreclosure sale is confirmed and turned into cash. Another ruling found that a trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a homestead claim meant to protect the proceeds of a voluntary sale from a judgment lien creditor.

So the exemption speaks to what an unsecured creditor can take. If the problem is a mortgage in default, the options are a loan modification, a sale, or a deal with the lender, and a cash sale can close faster than a listing. Talk with an attorney or a HUD-approved housing counselor before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Property tax breaks that work like a homestead exemption
sections.html:
Connecticut's property tax exemptions for owners are listed in section 12-81 of the General Statutes. Several are fixed-dollar reductions in assessed value, and the ones that most resemble a homestead exemption depend on who the owner is.

  • Blind residents: property to the amount of $3,000 under subdivision (17).
  • Wartime military service: property to the amount of $1,000 under subdivision (19).
  • Service members with disability ratings: property up to $3,500 under subdivision (20).

These carry filing rules in other sections, and there are limits when a person qualifies under more than one category. Your town assessor takes the application, so call that office for forms and deadlines. The circuit breaker credit also runs through the assessor.

sections.h2: Conveyance tax relief for distressed sellers
sections.html:
A tax relief program can change the conveyance tax at sale. The Department of Revenue Services lists an exemption from the state conveyance tax for the principal residence of a seller who is approved for property tax assistance under section 12-129b or 12-170aa for the current assessment year, or who was approved within the prior 15 months or less. That deed is not exempt from the municipal portion. An estate of a person who was approved for tax assistance cannot claim this exemption.

The same list covers other cases that come up in distressed sales.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on the seller's principal residence.
  • A principal residence that sells for less than the mortgages and senior tax liens against it.
  • A principal residence with a pyrrhotite crumbling foundation, when an engineer has put the evaluation in writing and the owner gets no money from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund. Only the first transfer after that written evaluation is exempt.

sections.h2: Conveyance tax when a house is sold
sections.html:
Under section 12-494 the state takes three-quarters of one percent of the price at the base rate, and the municipality takes another one-quarter of one percent. Nothing is owed on a deed with consideration under $2,000. The state rate is higher, one and one-quarter percent, for property that is not residential, except unimproved land. Other rates apply to certain residential estates, so read the statute or ask the town clerk about a high-value sale.

PieceBase rateWho receives it
State portion0.75 percentState General Fund, remitted by the town clerk
Municipal portion0.25 percentThe town's general revenue

Form OP-236 goes in from the seller side, either by the grantor, an attorney or an authorized agent, and payment is made at recording. Many towns take the return and payment online through myCTREC. Elsewhere, mail or hand the paper form to the town clerk with a check payable to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

Towns have to revalue real property on a five-year cycle under section 12-62, following a state schedule for each revaluation zone that starts October 1, 2023. A revalued house can land on a number far from the old one.

Disagree with a new value? Take it to the town's board of assessment appeals. A person aggrieved by that board's action can apply to the Superior Court no later than two months after the notice of the action was mailed, under section 12-117a.

Late payments are costly. Whatever is delinquent accrues interest at 18 percent a year from the due date. Each installment has a two-dollar minimum charge, which a town may choose to waive. At closing the collector's balance plus interest is normally paid out of your proceeds, so get a payoff figure early.

sections.h2: Checklist before selling a home with debts
sections.html:
List every debt and every recorded claim on the house. A title search turns up mortgages and liens, and the town tax collector states the tax balance. Then work through these steps.

  1. Confirm whether you live in the house as your primary residence, because that decides whether the creditor shield can apply.
  2. Ask your assessor whether you qualify for any exemption or the circuit breaker credit before the next filing window.
  3. Request a payoff from each mortgage lender and from the tax collector.
  4. Check which conveyance tax exemption, if any, matches your sale, and note its code.
  5. Speak with a Connecticut attorney if a judgment creditor is involved, since an exemption claim in court has its own procedure.

A cash sale leaves these rules as they are. It changes the timeline and removes repairs and showings.

faqs.q: Is there a property tax homestead exemption in Connecticut?
faqs.a: Connecticut's statutes use the word homestead for a creditor shield of $250,000 in section 52-352b(21). Property tax relief comes from named programs such as the circuit breaker credit and the exemptions in section 12-81. Ask your town assessor which one fits you.

faqs.q: Can a creditor force the sale of my Connecticut home?
faqs.a: A judgment creditor can pursue equity above the exempt amount, and a mortgage lender is not limited by the exemption at all. Equity under $250,000 in a primary residence is protected from ordinary judgment collection. A lawyer can say how a given debt is treated.

faqs.q: Do I have to live in the house for the exemption to count?
faqs.a: Yes. The statute defines a homestead as owner-occupied property used as a primary residence, so a rental or a second home does not qualify. A person who inherited a house and lives elsewhere should not assume the shield applies.

faqs.q: Who files the conveyance tax return when I sell?
faqs.a: The seller, or the seller's attorney or agent, completes Form OP-236. Take it to the town clerk when the deed is recorded, or file through myCTREC if your town accepts it, and pay any tax then.

faqs.q: Where do I apply for a military or blind exemption?
faqs.a: Apply with your town assessor. Section 12-81 sets the dollar amounts, and the assessor's office has the forms and the filing dates for your town.
